title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: what moves, what refuses to move, and who is speaking

questions.prompt: At the science fair of Kairouan, two visitors questioned Sami about the weather station he had built. The first asked him: "How do you store the readings?" The second asked him: "Do you work on it alone?" The next morning Sami tells his teacher what the two of them wanted to know. Which line reports both questions correctly?

options.text: One visitor asked me how did I store the readings, and the other asked me did I work on it alone.
One visitor asked me if I stored the readings, and the other asked me if I worked on it alone.
One visitor asked me how I stored the readings, and the other asked me if I worked on it alone.
One visitor asked me how was I storing the readings, and the other asked me whether did I work on it alone.

questions.explanation: One visitor asked me how I stored the readings, and the other asked me if I worked on it alone is right, and it is right twice over. A reported question stops being a question: it takes the word order of a statement and drops the do, does or did of the original, so how do you store becomes how I stored. A wh- question keeps its own question word, how; a yes/no question has no question word of its own and must borrow if, or whether, which is just as correct here. And since Sami reports the next morning, asked is a past, so store and work both step back to stored and worked, while you, who was Sami, becomes I. One visitor asked me how did I store the readings, and the other asked me did I work on it alone keeps the interrogative machinery in both halves, as if the inverted commas were still there. One visitor asked me if I stored the readings, and the other asked me if I worked on it alone is correctly built and reports the wrong question: if turns the first half into a yes or no, when the visitor did not ask whether Sami stored the readings but how he did it, and the question word how is the very thing a wh- question keeps. And One visitor asked me how was I storing the readings, and the other asked me whether did I work on it alone inverts the subject in the first half and keeps did after whether in the second: whether and if are followed by a statement, never by a question.

questions.prompt: On Monday, four members of the club each said one sentence. On Friday the secretary writes them all up, and each time she begins with the same three words, She said that. In which of the four sentences does the whole verb group stay exactly as it is?

options.text: I ought to check the cables before the concert.
I am drawing the plan of the new laboratory this evening.
I have booked the room for the second session.
I will fetch the spare battery from the office.

questions.explanation: I ought to check the cables before the concert is the one: ought to belongs to the small group of modals that have nowhere to step back to, with would, should, had better, might, used to, could and must, and the whole group is written in the report exactly as it was said, She said that she ought to check the cables. The other three all move, and each one shows a different line of the table. I am drawing the plan of the new laboratory this evening is a present continuous, and after a past reporting verb it becomes a past continuous, she was drawing. I have booked the room for the second session is a present perfect, which steps back one notch to she had booked. And I will fetch the spare battery from the office is a future, and a future reported from the past becomes she would fetch; will is exactly the modal that does move, which is why learning the short list of those that do not is worth as much as learning the table. Read the question carefully: in those three, one piece of the group does stay put, the drawing, the booked, the fetch. Only in the first does nothing at all change.

questions.prompt: Last week, in front of the whole club, Rania said: "I have lost my password twice since September." Today it is Rania herself who is writing the club's report, and she has to put that sentence of her own into it. Which line does the job?

options.text: She said that I had lost my password twice since September.
I said that I had lost my password twice since September.
Rania said that I had lost her password twice since September.
I said that she had lost her password twice since September.

questions.explanation: I said that I had lost my password twice since September is right. The pronouns and the possessives of a report move to the third person because the person speaking is no longer the person writing, and here those two people are the same woman: Rania is reporting her own words, so I and my stay exactly where they were. The tense moves in the ordinary way, since said is a past. I said that she had lost her password twice since September is the trap the rule is made for: it applies the third person mechanically and hands Rania's password to somebody else. She said that I had lost my password twice since September turns the writer into a third person while keeping the first person inside the report, so the reader is told that some other woman lost the writer's password. And Rania said that I had lost her password twice since September commits both faults at once, naming Rania outside the report and leaving I inside it.

questions.prompt: The grammar table of lesson 26 gives a second way of building the same gradual change: the comparative of the adjective, then and, then the same comparative again. The table prints that line without a single example beside it. Every machine the school buys does more in a second than the one bought before it, and the difference has not stopped growing. Which of these four sentences builds the pattern correctly?

options.text: The machines of the school laboratory are getting more and more fast.
The machines of the school laboratory are getting faster and fast.
The machines of the school laboratory are getting fast and faster.
The machines of the school laboratory are getting faster and faster.

questions.explanation: The machines of the school laboratory are getting faster and faster is right on both counts: fast has one syllable, so its comparative is faster and not more fast, and the structure repeats that comparative whole on each side of and. The machines of the school laboratory are getting more and more fast builds the comparative with more, which English keeps for the longer adjectives, more and more crowded, more and more expensive; with a short adjective it is the ending -er that carries the comparison. The machines of the school laboratory are getting faster and fast and The machines of the school laboratory are getting fast and faster each leave one half in the plain form, and half a structure carries none of its meaning: both sides of and have to be comparatives, which is the whole idea of two comparatives joined by and.

questions.prompt: Four sentences from a science page, each using one word of the lesson. In one of them the word is used in a way its meaning does not allow, and the sentence contradicts itself. Which one?

options.text: The engineer assumes that the two machines will behave in the same way.
Two of the three prototypes survived the whole of the heat test.
A substantial number of the batteries, four out of six hundred, were sent back.
The reason for the fall in the price of memory is obvious in the second column of the table.

questions.explanation: A substantial number of the batteries, four out of six hundred, were sent back is the sentence that breaks: substantial means large in size or in amount, and the very figures the sentence gives, four out of six hundred, are as small as a number can well be. The writer meant a tiny number, or a handful, and chose a word that says the opposite. The other three use their word exactly as the lesson does. The engineer assumes that the two machines will behave in the same way takes something as true without having proved it, which is what assume is for. Two of the three prototypes survived the whole of the heat test says they came through a hard test without being destroyed. And The reason for the fall in the price of memory is obvious in the second column of the table says the reason can be seen there without anybody explaining it.

questions.prompt: The phrasal verb break up carries several everyday senses, and only the words standing round it say which one is meant. In which of these four sentences does it mean that a relationship between two people has come to an end?

options.text: The ice on the reservoir broke up in the first week of March.
They broke up last spring, after two years together.
The class broke up into four groups for the experiment.
The signal broke up in the tunnel and we lost the call.

questions.explanation: They broke up last spring, after two years together carries the sense the lesson uses: two people whose relationship comes to an end. Nothing in the verb says so; everything that decides it stands beside it, two years together, which can only be said of people. The ice on the reservoir broke up in the first week of March is the most concrete sense of all, a solid sheet coming apart into pieces, and the first week of March tells you why it happened. The class broke up into four groups for the experiment is the sense a gathering takes when it separates into smaller parts, and into four groups names the parts. And The signal broke up in the tunnel and we lost the call describes a sound or a picture becoming broken and unclear, the sense you meet on a telephone. One verb, four senses, and no way to choose between them except by reading what stands beside it.
